extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of classical mechanics; readers studying Huygens/Galileo-level dynamics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted principles and operative formulas from a textbook chapter on dynamics (projection, centripetal force, pendula, Huygens' results). Useful for learning/teaching and applying classical dynamics laws and experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of projection (range formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: The horizontal range w of a projectile launched with speed c at angle a is w = (c^2/g) . sin 2a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: horizontal motion during ascent+descent; ascent time t = c sin a / g, horizontal velocity c cos a, so w = c cos a · 2t = (c^2/g) sin 2a. Consequence: range maximal when a = 45° and equal for complementary angles (a and 90°−a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual independence (superposition) of motions/forces
rubrics_metrics.description: If two circumstances (forces or motion-determinative circumstances) simultaneously determine motions and have no influence on one another, their effects compound vectorially (parallelogram law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to displacements, velocities and accelerations: a body moving AB while its space is displaced AC goes to D; when the two determining circumstances do not interact we may compound motions by the parallelogram. (See Appendix reference.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Centripetal vs. centrifugal force conceptualization
rubrics_metrics.description: When a body is swung in a circle by a string, the tension of the string is the centripetal force acting on the body; the equal and opposite reaction on the axis/centre appears as a centrifugal force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: stone on a string — tension constantly deflects body from rectilinear path toward centre (centripetal). The axis experiences equal opposite action (centrifugal). This frames understanding of circular motion forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centripetal acceleration ∝ (velocity)^2 in equal circles
rubrics_metrics.description: In equal circles the centripetal acceleration is proportional to the square of the velocity of the motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument using corresponding small arc-elements and Galileo's law of falling bodies: for equal arcs and proportional velocities (1:2) corresponding departures from tangents show cp1 = 4 cp2 etc., giving cp ∝ v^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: For equal velocities, centripetal acceleration ∝ 1/radius
rubrics_metrics.description: When the velocity of circular motion is the same in two circles, the centripetal acceleration is inversely proportional to the radius of the circle described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by comparing motions in circles of radii in ratio 1:2 with velocities chosen so arc-elements match in equal times; reducing velocity in larger circle shows inverse proportionality to radius.

rubrics_metrics.name: General formula for centripetal acceleration (v^2/r and alternate forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Centripetal (or centrifugal) acceleration cp = v^2 / r. Using period T, cp = 4π^2 r / T^2. Also for small-angle derivations tan a ≈ a = cp r / v^2 leading to cp = v^2 / r as complete expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate forms are useful: cp expressed via v and r or via period T (vT = 2πr ⇒ cp = 4π^2 r/T^2). If several bodies have same T, cp ∝ r. Small-angle approximations and geometric decomposition are used in derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradoxical character of constant centripetal acceleration
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniform circular motion maintained by a constant centripetal acceleration seems paradoxical because there is no actual approach to centre and no increase of speed, despite constant inward-directed acceleration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolution: the direction of acceleration continually changes; without the centripetal acceleration the body would move away from centre. More complex central motions (elliptical) further elucidate this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrifugal effects explain apparent variations in gravity (pendulum clock example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pendulum-clock retardation observed when taken from Paris to Cayenne is explained by greater centrifugal acceleration of rotating Earth at equator, producing apparent diminution of g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concept that rotating Earth adds outward centrifugal acceleration, altering effective g; Huygens applied centripetal/centrifugal conception to explain Richer's observed retarding of pendulum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-angle pendulum approximation: acceleration ∝ displacement (simple harmonic)
rubrics_metrics.description: For small oscillations of a pendulum of length l, the restoring acceleration is g·sin a ≈ g·a (for small a), so acceleration is proportional to excursion and opposite in direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model pendulum bob motion as descent on an inclined plane/chord; neglect curvature for small excursions. This is the basis for simple harmonic motion approximations and obtaining period formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period of small oscillations independent of amplitude
rubrics_metrics.description: For the class of oscillatory motions with acceleration proportional to displacement (as above), the period of oscillation is independent of the amplitude (for small oscillations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument via dividing amplitudes into many elements: scaling shows corresponding times match when amplitudes scale, or via Newtonian similarity principles (phoronomical similarity). Experimental consequence: pendulum period unaffected by small change in amplitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period of oscillation scales with acceleration and length (laws of oscillation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For equal excursions, the time of oscillation is inversely proportional to the square root of the acceleration; for pendulum T ∝ sqrt(l/g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivations given via element comparisons and similarity arguments. Newton's method of similarity: homologous paths/times yield ft = sqrt(a_i/a_j) relations and yield T = 2π sqrt(l/g) for small pendulum vibrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of dynamical similarity (phoronomical similarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Material systems geometrically similar and with homologous masses in same ratio execute similar movements when homologous points describe similar paths in proportional times; homologous velocities scale as s/t and accelerations as s/t^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using scaling factors for lengths, times, velocities, accelerations one obtains general scaling laws for oscillations and centripetal acceleration theorems. Useful for generalisation and converting results between similar systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection between circular uniform motion and simple oscillatory motion (projections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniform circular motion can be resolved into two independent orthogonal oscillatory motions: the x- and y-components are simple oscillations about the centre with accelerations proportional to excursion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve centripetal acceleration into components; each component acts independently on corresponding coordinate, yielding SHM with period equal to circular motion period. Leads to T = 2π sqrt(1/f) where f = cp/r is acceleration per unit excursion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendulum period formula and experimental verification
rubrics_metrics.description: For small oscillations of a simple pendulum, T = 2π sqrt(l/g). Experimental checks: pendulums of lengths in ratio 1:4:9 have periods 1:2:3 respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental setups and methods described (double threads to keep plane, varying lengths). Verifying g dependence is harder but can be addressed by altering effective component of g (inclined plane of oscillation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of period on effective component of gravity (inclined-axis pendulum)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plane of oscillation is inclined so only component g·cosβ acts in that plane, the period becomes T = 2π sqrt(l/(g cos β)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment: rotate pendulum axis by angle β; as β increases effective acceleration decreases and period increases. If plane becomes horizontal, oscillation period tends to infinity (no return). Apparatus described (frame hinged, graduated arc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conical pendulum relations
rubrics_metrics.description: For a conical pendulum of length l at cone angle α, centrifugal acceleration must balance component of gravity: cp/g = tan α. Period T = 2π sqrt(l cos α / g). For very small α, T ≈ 2π sqrt(l/g) (one revolution corresponds to two small oscillations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Velocity v = sqrt(g l sin α tan α) and v = (2π r)/T with r = l sin α. Use these relations to compute periods and velocities; small-angle simplification connects to regular pendulum formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of g by pendulum (Huygens' method)
rubrics_metrics.description: From T = 2π sqrt(l/g) we obtain g = 4π^2 l / T^2; Huygens used pendulum observations to determine g (e.g., g ≈ 9.806 m/s^2 at latitude 45°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: units matter — g is length divided by time^2; formula yields g in metres/second^2 if l in metres and T in seconds. For rough mental calculations, g ≈ 10 m/s^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Huygens' principle for centre of oscillation (conservation of centre-of-gravity-rise under dissolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Velocities impressed on the particles of a connected pendulum during descent are such that, whether connections remain or are dissolved, the center of gravity of the particles can rise to the same height as the point from which it fell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huygens argued that dissolving connections at maximum displacement and letting particles rise cannot make the centre of gravity ascend higher than initial point (otherwise perpetual motion). This principle underlies the definition and determination of the centre of oscillation and generalises Galileo's ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and existence of centre of oscillation for a compound pendulum
rubrics_metrics.description: A compound pendulum (extended body free to rotate about an axis) has a point (centre of oscillation) such that if the length of a simple pendulum equal to the distance to that point is taken, it has the same period as the compound pendulum; the centre preserves the same period whether connected or detached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive reasoning: consider many constituent masses at various distances; when freed at maximum velocities their individual ascents produce same overall center-of-gravity height—this determines a unique effective length and the locus of the centre of oscillation. Huygens provided general solution and remarks on method.
